content: The MeNZB vaccine is specifically designed to protect against a particular strain of group B meningococcus. It is currently being utilized in New Zealand to manage an ongoing epidemic of meningococcal disease. While most individuals can carry the meningococcus bacteria without experiencing any adverse effects, meningococcal disease can lead to severe conditions such as meningitis and septicaemia. These conditions may result in brain damage, multi-organ failure, extensive skin and soft tissue damage, and even death. The immunization process with the MeNZB vaccine requires three doses, administered approximately six weeks apart. For newborns, the doses are given alongside their routine 6-week, 3-month, and 5-month vaccinations. However, even individuals who are fully immunized may still carry the meningococcus bacteria and remain susceptible to contracting meningococcal disease. The vaccine contains 65 mg of aluminum hydroxide, which acts as an adjuvant, and histidine, which stabilizes the pH. It also includes normal saline to dissolve the components into an injectable solution. Importantly, the vaccine does not contain any whole bacteria, whether alive or dead. Instead, it includes outer membrane vesicles, which are small fragments of the bacterial outer membrane. These vesicles help the immune system recognize and prepare for potential infection by the actual bacteria. The MeNZB vaccine does not contain any human, blood, bovine (cow), or egg products, nor does it include neomycin or the preservative thiomersal (mercury). There are no live meningococcal bacteria in the vaccine, making it impossible to contract the disease or become a carrier from receiving the vaccine. The immune system typically does not respond to the outer membrane vesicles when presented alone. However, the presence of the adjuvant ensures an immune response by preventing the breakdown and elimination of the vesicles. The adjuvant also induces localized tissue damage to provoke the desired immune reaction. The histidine pH buffer ensures the vaccine remains close to the pH of human body fluids, preventing the immune system from wasting resources neutralizing the vaccine instead of responding to the vesicles. The saline solution, which matches the salinity of human body fluids, serves as a medium to dissolve the vaccine components for injection. The vaccine is derived from the N. meningitidis strain NZ98/254, which is cultivated in a fermentor using a synthetic culture medium. This medium contains sugar, essential amino acids, and elements like iron and potassium. No bovine or porcine products are used in the fermentation process. The bacterial outer membranes are extracted using the detergent deoxycholate, which kills the bacteria. The outer membrane vesicles are then purified from the culture medium through ultracentrifugation, stabilized with histidine, and adsorbed onto aluminum hydroxide as an adjuvant. Further purification is achieved through ultrafiltration and diafiltration. Since its introduction, the MeNZB vaccine has had a significant impact on controlling the epidemic in New Zealand. The vaccine was originally developed in Norway but was not widely released there because the Norwegian epidemic subsided before its deployment. Additionally, Norwegian authorities never approved their version of the vaccine for use in infants and babies.
